newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi plans tightening of civil controls.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi plans tightening of civil controls.

text.p: Authorities in Vietnam's capital said on Saturday they were planning to tighten civil controls, including measures to manage demonstrations and closer monitoring of dissidents and foreigners.
The announcement in the official Hanoi Moi newspaper said new circumstances and Hanoi's special role as the country's capital demanded a readjustment of security measures.
It said a two-day meeting in the past week of the executive board of the Hanoi Party Committee had decided that attention needed to be paid to a range of emerging problems.
The published list included political opportunism, activities involving foreigners, demonstrations and social vices.
An official at the Hanoi Party Committee office told Reuters no specific event had prompted the move but explained the measures were needed to address a changing situation in the city.
He said the authorities were concerned that "ringleaders" were seeking to stir up trouble at demonstrations -- rare, but increasing events in Vietnam.
"Those incidents do not violate the law but they cause social and traffic disorder," he said.
The recent trials of leading dissidents Hoang Minh Chinh and Le Hong Ha indicated a threat from political opportunists, he said.
Le Hong Ha, a former ranking interior ministry official, was jailed in August for two years on charges of divulging state secrets.
He had been expelled from the ruling Communist Party after voicing support for Hoang Minh Chinh, a veteran party critic who was released from prison in June.
The official, who declined to be identified, said the authorities were also seeking to tighten police monitoring of foreigners in the capital and of Vietnamese nationals travelling abroad.
Vietnam introduced economic reforms and an open-door policy in the late 1980s following years of international isolation prompted by its 1978 invasion of Cambodia.
The result has been an economic lift-off, dramatic social changes and a new acceptance of the communist-run country by the international community.
Despite the successes, critics within the Communist Party have pointed to the emergence of what they say are undesirable side-effects resulting from these policies.
Saturday's announcement also referred to the need to combat "social evils, which are now on the rise under various forms".

Traditionally, these refer to gambling, prostitution and narcotics, but in the past year the list has been expanded to include items such as compact discs, videos and magazines containing material seen as harmful to Vietnamese culture.
The announcement said the measures were aimed at ensuring the political security, social order and safety of the capital.
